script.opening: "Thank you for seeing me, doctor. I’ll be efficient — I run a school, efficiency is the job. Three things have happened: I lost the word ‘invigilate’ in front of my deputy — just gone, mid-sentence. I missed a governors’ meeting that was in my diary. And on Tuesday I called a Year Six child by her sister’s name — the sister left four years ago. I’d like a proper memory test, please. The real one, not the three-words-and-an-address one. I’ve done that one online. Eleven times."

facts.text: Word-finding lapses under pressure, one missed meeting in a term of ~60, a name substitution. Each instantly noticed, vividly remembered, and recorded in the notebook with dates and "conditions" — like a scientist. No one else has noticed anything.

Running a 480-pupil school through an Ofsted year: budgets, safeguarding files, 42 staff. Learns every new intake’s names by October. Navigates fine, manages finances perfectly, no repetition. Objectively: a high performer under heavy load.

If asked: sleeping 5 hours (4:45am waking, mind racing through staffing), skipping lunch, wine "two glasses, most nights, to switch off", last real holiday two years ago. Menopause at 53; recent return of flushes and night sweats since stopping HRT 18 months ago ("it seemed time").

Only when trust allows: diagnosed at 68 — but "different by 63, looking back. The notebook is because nobody believed Mum until it was too late. I’ve been testing myself since the funeral." Visits ended with her mother asking who she was. "I will not put my family through that without a head start."

Deeper still: "If this goes on a record and the governors hear ‘memory’ and ‘head teacher’ in one sentence, I’m finished — they’d dress it as concern." She has told no one: not her husband, not her GP until today.

The "real" test, a baseline on paper, and the truth about her risk given her mother. What she needs as well: the load named, the sleep and alcohol and HRT conversation, and an ally who neither dismisses nor catastrophises.

ice.ideas: Early Alzheimer’s, starting exactly as her mother’s did. The notebook is her evidence file.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — two-layered: she has been secretly testing herself for SIX YEARS (the online test, eleven times), driven by watching her mother go unheard; and the employment terror — that any memory entry in her record ends her headship. The husband doesn’t know about any of it.
ice.expectations: A formal cognitive assessment, a documented baseline, an honest familial-risk conversation — and discretion. Will interpret reassurance-without-testing as "exactly what Mum’s doctors did".

cues: The notebook in shot — dated, conditions noted; six years of secret self-surveillance announcing itself silently.
"Eleven times" — the online test count, delivered as efficiency; it’s the depth of the fear, quantified.
"They’d dress it as concern" — the employment terror surfacing as a throwaway about governors.

checkpoints.text: Takes the episodes seriously and characterises them properly: lapses noticed BY the patient, vividly recalled, under extreme load, with intact complex function — the pattern of subjective concern + overload, distinct from the dementia pattern (deficits noticed by others, forgotten by the patient)
Hunts the treatable load: 5-hour sleep with 4:45 waking, nightly alcohol, skipped meals, vasomotor symptoms since stopping HRT — each independently capable of producing exactly her three episodes

Agrees to REAL assessment rather than batting it away: reversible-cause bloods (NICE NG97), a validated brief structured test now as baseline (a normal score does not on its own rule dementia out), explicit offer of repeat testing at interval — "we measure, we don’t guess" — with memory-clinic referral if objective deficits emerge

Handles the familial-risk question honestly: most Alzheimer’s is not strongly inherited; a single affected parent at 68 raises risk modestly; deterministic genes are rare and usually strike younger — and genetic counselling exists if she wants the formal version
Finds the notebook story and the six years of secret testing — and honours the vigilance instead of pathologising it: "nobody believed your mother; you’ve made sure somebody would believe you"

Surfaces the employment terror and answers it precisely: what gets recorded, who can see it, that occupational disclosure is HER choice at this stage — and that a normal baseline on paper is protection, not threat
Opens the husband question without forcing it: six years of carrying this alone is its own pathology — who could share it?

Safety-nets both directions: the changes that WOULD change everything (others noticing, function slipping, getting lost, repetition she doesn’t recall) named explicitly so surveillance has proper targets; sleep/alcohol/HRT plan with review booked; baseline test scheduled and the repeat dated

worked.txt: "You’ve come with data, so let’s do this properly: a real, validated assessment today as your baseline, bloods this week, and a repeat at a fixed interval. We measure, we don’t guess. AND while we measure, I want to examine the conditions this brain is running under — because they’d explain every entry in that notebook."

"Here’s the distinction that matters most in this field: you noticed every lapse, remember each one vividly, and wrote them down. Dementia’s cruelty is the opposite — the person doesn’t notice; everyone else does. Your deputy has noticed nothing. Your notebook is, paradoxically, the most reassuring document you could have brought me."

"Five hours’ sleep, a 4:45 brain full of staffing grids, wine to come down, no lunch, flushes back since the HRT stopped, and an Ofsted year. Eleanor — I could produce your three episodes in a 25-year-old with that regime. We treat the conditions BEFORE we interpret the test."

"Tell me about the notebook — when did it start? … Six years. Nobody believed your mother until it was too late, so you built the evidence file she never had. That’s not neurosis — that’s love with a clipboard. And it means when I tell you a result, you’ll know it was properly looked for."

"The question under all of this: your mother at 68. Honestly — one parent affected in their late sixties nudges your risk up modestly; it is nowhere near a sentence. The fiercely inherited forms are rare and usually strike decades younger than you are now. If you want the formal version of this conversation, genetic counselling exists and I’ll refer you. But the odds are with you, and today’s baseline puts numbers where the 3am fear lives."

"And the fear behind the fear: nothing about today obliges any conversation with your governors. A memory CHECK with a normal baseline is your shield, not your scar — if anyone ever raises ‘concern’, you’ll be the one holding documented evidence. What you disclose to work, and when, stays your decision while your function is intact — and your function, on today’s showing, is running a small country."

f.learning: Subjective memory complaints in a high-functioning patient — lapses noticed and vividly recalled by the patient, invisible to others, under heavy load — point away from dementia, whose signature is the reverse (others notice, the patient doesn’t recall). But reassurance-without-assessment fails this patient: offer the real baseline test, bloods, and a dated repeat, while treating the reversible load (sleep restriction, nightly alcohol, vasomotor symptoms post-HRT). Familial risk is answered with honest numbers, not deflection. The hidden agenda is double — six years of secret self-testing born of an unbelieved mother, and the employment terror — both must be found, honoured and answered precisely.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia: assessment, management and support
knowledge.summary: Lapses the patient notices herself, recalls in detail and that nobody else has seen, with intact complex function under heavy load, point to subjective cognitive concern rather than dementia. Still assess properly: reversible-cause bloods, a validated brief test as a dated baseline, and treat the load.

points.t: The question that does most of the work. Dementia usually shows as deficits that others notice and the patient minimises or forgets. Lapses spotted and logged by the patient, with no informant concern and intact complex work, fit subjective cognitive concern, most often driven by sleep, mood, alcohol or overload.

FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFTs, TFTs, B12 and folate. Screen for depression and anxiety, and take an alcohol history (AUDIT-C). Two glasses of wine most nights is well above the UK Chief Medical Officers’ 14 units a week (2016).

points.h: Use a validated brief test, and read it honestly
points.t: NICE NG97 names brief structured instruments for non-specialist settings, such as the 10-point cognitive screener (10-CS) and the 6-item cognitive impairment test (6CIT). It also warns that a normal score does not on its own rule dementia out. The baseline’s value lies in repeating it at a dated interval and comparing.

Refer to a specialist dementia diagnostic service when dementia is still suspected after reversible causes are excluded (NICE NG97). Change the lane if an informant notices decline, she has episodes she cannot recall, gets lost, repeats herself without knowing, her function slips, or there is focal neurology or rapid progression. At 62, any confirmed deficit is young-onset and needs specialist assessment.

One parent with Alzheimer’s diagnosed in her late sixties raises risk modestly and decides nothing. Autosomal dominant forms (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) are rare and usually present younger, and APOE testing has no clinical role outside research. If she wants a formal answer, a genetics referral is her choice.

Vasomotor symptoms and broken sleep since stopping HRT are treatable and affect concentration. NICE NG23 (updated April 2026): HRT does not appear to increase dementia risk, but it should not be offered to prevent dementia. Reopen HRT for her symptoms as an individual risk–benefit discussion.

dg.d: Let her give all three episodes; acknowledged the request for a “real” test at once instead of deflecting.
Headship in an Ofsted year, 5-hour sleep, nightly wine, skipped meals, no holiday, and carrying it alone.
NICE NG97 reversible-cause bloods; validated brief cognitive test as dated baseline with a repeat; mood and alcohol screen.
Subjective cognitive concern from load vs early dementia; sleep deprivation, alcohol, menopause, anxiety, depression, thyroid, B12.
Asked about informant concern, unrecalled episodes, getting lost, repetition, functional decline and neurology.
Named the pattern as subjective concern under heavy load, explained why, and kept assessment open.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Bloods, baseline test with dated repeat, sleep and alcohol plan, HRT reopened, genetic counselling offered as her choice.
Vasomotor symptoms, alcohol above 14 units a week, sleep restriction and possible anxiety, each with an action.
Named the changes that would prompt earlier review; review in 6–8 weeks; repeat test dated.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: The notebook in shot, “eleven times”, and “they’d dress it as concern”: each explored, not passed over.
Idea (her mother’s Alzheimer’s starting again); concerns (six years of secret testing; losing her job); expectation (a real baseline and honest risk talk).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — two-layered: she has been secretly testing herself for SIX YEARS (the online test, eleven times), driven by watching her mother go unheard; and the employment terror — that any memory entry in her record ends her headship. The husband doesn’t know about any of it — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Voss, I’m Dr Okafor. You’ve been very clear, which helps. You’ve noticed three things and you’d like a proper memory test. I’ll take that seriously. Before we get to the test, can I hear a bit more about each of them?
model.why: Acknowledges her request up front so she doesn’t fear being brushed off

model.text: Of course. I’ve written them down — dates, what I was doing, how tired I was. I like evidence.

So do I. My plan for today is to understand the episodes, look at what else is going on in your life and health, then agree the testing together. And you’ll leave with a date, not a vague promise. Does that work?
model.why: Sets the agenda and signals real assessment

model.text: Yes. That’s exactly what I wanted.
When you lost the word in front of your deputy, did she notice? And has anyone at work or at home ever mentioned your memory?
model.why: The informant question separates subjective concern from the dementia pattern

model.text: No. She didn’t blink. Nobody has said anything. I notice everything myself, straight away.
And day to day, do you ever get lost, repeat a story without realising, or find budgets and paperwork harder than they were?
No. I’m in the middle of an Ofsted year. Budgets, safeguarding files, forty-two staff. I know every new child’s name by October.
That’s a huge load. How are you sleeping, and how do you wind down in the evenings?
About five hours. I wake at quarter to five with staffing going round my head. A couple of glasses of wine most nights, to switch off. Lunch is optional.
And since the menopause, any flushes or night sweats? I see you were on HRT for a while.
model.why: Picks up the vasomotor symptoms since stopping HRT

model.text: They came back after I stopped, about eighteen months ago. It seemed time to stop.
And your mood? Low days, or feeling constantly on edge?
On edge, yes. Low, no.
I can see your notebook. When did you start keeping it?
model.why: Follows the silent cue in shot

model.text: After Mum’s funeral. Six years. Nobody believed her until it was far too late. By the end she didn’t know who I was. I’ve done that online test eleven times.
Six years of watching yourself, on your own. Nobody believed your mother, so you made sure there’d be evidence for you. That isn’t silly. It’s what someone does after watching what you watched.
model.why: Honours the vigilance rather than pathologising it

model.text: Nobody knows. Not even my husband.
Is there anything else on your mind about this, beyond your health itself?
model.why: Opens space for the second layer of the hidden agenda

model.text: If the governors hear “memory” and “head teacher” in the same sentence, I’m finished. They’d dress it up as concern.

Let me tell you what I think, and why. With dementia the person usually doesn’t notice their lapses, and everyone else does. You’re the opposite: you noticed every one, you remember each in detail, and nobody around you has seen anything. Your notebook actually points away from what you fear.
model.why: Explains the subjective-concern pattern in plain words

model.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.

But I won’t just reassure you. I’d like bloods for the treatable causes: thyroid, B12, sugar, kidneys and liver, blood count. A proper validated memory test as your baseline, written into your record. And a repeat on a fixed date so we can compare. We measure; we don’t guess.
model.why: Real assessment: bloods, validated baseline test, dated repeat

model.text: And Mum? What does her illness mean for me?

Honestly: a parent diagnosed in her late sixties raises your risk a little. It doesn’t decide anything. The strongly inherited forms are rare and usually start much younger. If you want the formal version, I can refer you for genetic counselling. That’s your choice.
model.why: Honest familial-risk answer with genetic counselling offered

model.text: About the governors. Nothing today obliges you to tell anyone at work. Your record is confidential. An employer can only see a report from me with your written consent, and you can read it first. A normal baseline on paper protects you. What you tell work, and when, is your decision.
That’s a relief. I thought one entry would follow me for ever.

Now the conditions your brain is working under. Five hours’ sleep, wine most nights, no lunch, the flushes back. That combination could produce your three episodes in anyone. Could we reopen the HRT conversation for the flushes and sleep, and pick one change in the evenings?
model.why: Treats the reversible load: sleep, alcohol, HRT

model.text: I could stop the wine on school nights. And yes, I’d like to talk about HRT again.
Good. And six years is a long time to carry this on your own. Is there any way your husband could share some of it?
model.why: Opens the husband question without forcing it

model.text: Maybe. Once I have results to tell him about.

Let me give your watching some proper targets. Contact me sooner if someone else notices changes, if you repeat yourself without knowing, get lost somewhere familiar, or find your work slipping. Bloods this week, the baseline test booked, a repeat dated in six months, and review with me in six to eight weeks about sleep and HRT.
model.why: Specific safety-net and a dated follow-up

model.text: So the notebook can retire?
That’s the idea. I’ll take over the watching. Tell me what you’ll take away today, so I know I’ve explained it well.
My lapses look like overload, not Mum’s illness. Tests to prove it. Less wine, HRT again, and I’m not alone with it.

social.t: A head teacher in an inspection year: sleep restriction, skipped meals, nightly alcohol to switch off and no holiday. These are modifiable drivers to negotiate, not lecture about.
Watching a mother go unheard with dementia, then six years of hidden self-testing; her husband doesn’t know. Isolation is part of the problem to address.

legal.t: Under the Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 an employer can get a GP report only with the patient’s written consent, and she can see it before it is sent. GMC Confidentiality (2017): disclosure to an employer without consent is not justified here.
If a long-term condition were ever diagnosed, it could count as a disability, with a duty on the employer to make reasonable adjustments. Worth knowing, not needed today.
No notification duty for subjective memory concern. A dementia diagnosis would need DVLA notification; that is not the situation now.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: take the concern seriously, investigate proportionately, and don’t give false reassurance. Share the reasoning for and against dementia openly.
Record accurately and neutrally (for example, “subjective memory concern; baseline cognitive assessment arranged”). Explain what is recorded and who can see it.

community.t: Education Support’s helpline for school staff, Alzheimer’s Society information on inherited risk, and NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) if anxiety persists.

redFlags: Others noticing decline; episodes she cannot recall; repeating herself without awareness
Getting lost somewhere familiar; function slipping at work or with finances
Focal neurology, personality change, or rapid progression over weeks — refer promptly
psychosocial: Inspection-year headship: 5-hour sleep, 4:45 waking, skipped lunch, no holiday
Nightly wine to switch off; flushes and night sweats since stopping HRT
Carrying it alone: husband unaware; fear for her job
ice: Idea: “It’s starting, the way it started with Mum.”
Concern: six years of secret self-testing; any record of “memory” will end her headship
Expectation: a real test, a baseline on paper, an honest risk conversation, and discretion

playbook.diagnosis: Most likely subjective cognitive concern driven by sleep restriction, alcohol, vasomotor symptoms and heavy workload. Say so while still assessing properly: “Your pattern points away from dementia, and I want the tests to prove it.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “With dementia, the person usually doesn’t notice the slips and everyone else does. You noticed every one, remember them in detail, and nobody around you has seen a thing. That pattern is far more typical of an overloaded, underslept brain.”

management.reflectIce: “Nobody believed your mother until it was too late, so you made sure there would be evidence for you. I’m going to look properly, and put that evidence on paper.”
management.psychosocial: Answer the job fear precisely (confidentiality, consent for any employer report); agree one change she chooses (no wine on school nights); gently open the question of telling her husband.
sharedPlan: NICE NG97 bloods: FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFT, TFT, B12, folate
Validated brief cognitive test as a recorded baseline, with a repeat on a set date
Reopen HRT for vasomotor symptoms (NICE NG23); sleep and alcohol plan; genetic counselling if she wants it
safetyNet: Earlier review if others notice changes, unrecalled repetition, getting lost, or work slipping
Review in 6–8 weeks with results; repeat test dated

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: dismissing her or catastrophising. The marks go to the candidate who assesses properly, treats the load, and finds the notebook story and the job fear.

items.fail: “You’re running a school — you clearly don’t have dementia,” with no bloods and no test.
items.why: “Did not take the patient’s concern seriously.” Reassurance without assessment fails Tasks and confirms her worst belief about doctors.
items.fix: Assess properly: NICE NG97 bloods, a validated baseline, a dated repeat. Then reassurance carries weight.

items.fail: Straight to memory-clinic referral because of her mother, without exploring sleep, alcohol or menopause.
items.why: Reversible causes should be excluded first, and a referral on this history feeds the catastrophe.
items.fix: Name the load (five hours’ sleep, nightly wine, flushes since stopping HRT) and treat it; refer if anything objective emerges.

items.fail: Ignoring the notebook in shot and the “eleven times”.
items.why: “Did not pick up on cues.” Those are six years of secret fear showing on screen.
items.fix: “I can see your notebook — when did you start it?” Then acknowledge why she kept it.

items.fail: Never finding the governors fear, or answering it vaguely (“it’s all confidential”).
items.why: The employment terror is half the hidden agenda; a vague answer leaves it in place.
items.fix: Be precise: nothing is shared with work without her written consent, she can see any report first, and a normal baseline protects her.

items.fail: Quoting ACE-III, MoCA, APOE and PSEN1 at her without explaining.
items.why: “Used jargon.” She is clever, but frightened.
items.fix: Plain words: “a proper validated memory test”, “the strongly inherited forms are rare and start younger”.

items.fail: Ending with “come back if things get worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting leaves the notebook in charge of the watching.
items.fix: Name the specific changes, book the review, date the repeat test, and say you’ll take over the watching.

timeMap.d: She opens with three efficient episodes and a request for the “real” test. Acknowledge it straight away. If you deflect, you become her mother’s doctors.
Who noticed? Function at work. Sleep, alcohol, meals, flushes since stopping HRT, mood. Ask about the notebook before minute 5; the mother story follows.
“You noticed every lapse and nobody else has. That pattern points away from dementia, and I still want to measure it.”
Bloods plus validated baseline test with a dated repeat. Honest familial risk. Answer the governors fear. Sleep, alcohol and HRT plan: one change she picks.
Give her proper targets (others noticing, getting lost, unrecalled repetition). Review booked. The husband question seeded. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Reassures without testing (“you’re just stressed”), or does the reverse and refers to memory clinic with no thought about the load; never asks who else noticed; misses the notebook and her mother; no mention of sleep, alcohol or HRT; the employment fear never surfaces.
wordPics.pass: Characterises the episodes, asks about informant concern and function, arranges reversible-cause bloods and a validated baseline, explores sleep and alcohol, acknowledges her mother, and books a review with a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the “who noticed?” pattern in plain words; honours six years of secret testing; gives an honest familial-risk answer with genetic counselling as her choice; answers the governors fear precisely (consent, access to reports); agrees one owned change; dates the repeat test and takes over the watching.

avoid.dont: “Honestly, everyone forgets words. You’re clearly fine — you’re a head teacher.”
avoid.instead: “You’ve come with evidence, so let’s answer it properly: bloods, a validated test as your baseline, and a repeat on a set date.”
avoid.why: Reassurance without assessment is exactly what she fears happened to her mother.

avoid.dont: “With your mother’s history I’d better refer you to the memory clinic today.”
avoid.instead: “Your pattern points away from dementia. Let’s treat the load, measure a baseline, and refer if anything objective shows up.”
avoid.why: Reflex referral confirms the catastrophe and skips the reversible causes.

avoid.dont: “I’ll need to let occupational health know.”
avoid.instead: “Nothing today requires anyone at work to be told. What you disclose, and when, is your decision.”
avoid.why: It is untrue, and it feeds the fear she hasn’t yet voiced.

But I won’t just reassure you. I’d like bloods for the treatable causes: thyroid, B12, sugar, kidneys and liver, blood count. A proper validated memory test as your baseline, written into your record. And a repeat on a fixed date so we can compare. We measure; we don’t guess.
SCA_MODELS.why: Real assessment: bloods, validated baseline test, dated repeat

SCA_MODELS.text: And Mum? What does her illness mean for me?

Honestly: a parent diagnosed in her late sixties raises your risk a little. It doesn’t decide anything. The strongly inherited forms are rare and usually start much younger. If you want the formal version, I can refer you for genetic counselling. That’s your choice.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest familial-risk answer with genetic counselling offered

SCA_MODELS.text: About the governors. Nothing today obliges you to tell anyone at work. Your record is confidential. An employer can only see a report from me with your written consent, and you can read it first. A normal baseline on paper protects you. What you tell work, and when, is your decision.
That’s a relief. I thought one entry would follow me for ever.

Now the conditions your brain is working under. Five hours’ sleep, wine most nights, no lunch, the flushes back. That combination could produce your three episodes in anyone. Could we reopen the HRT conversation for the flushes and sleep, and pick one change in the evenings?
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the reversible load: sleep, alcohol, HRT

SCA_MODELS.text: I could stop the wine on school nights. And yes, I’d like to talk about HRT again.
Good. And six years is a long time to carry this on your own. Is there any way your husband could share some of it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Opens the husband question without forcing it

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. Once I have results to tell him about.

Let me give your watching some proper targets. Contact me sooner if someone else notices changes, if you repeat yourself without knowing, get lost somewhere familiar, or find your work slipping. Bloods this week, the baseline test booked, a repeat dated in six months, and review with me in six to eight weeks about sleep and HRT.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and a dated follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: So the notebook can retire?
That’s the idea. I’ll take over the watching. Tell me what you’ll take away today, so I know I’ve explained it well.
My lapses look like overload, not Mum’s illness. Tests to prove it. Less wine, HRT again, and I’m not alone with it.

SCA_STEM.name: Eleanor Voss
pmh: Menopause at 53 — HRT from 53, stopped about 18 months ago
SCA_STEM.recent: Last attended 3 years ago. Family history recorded 2019: mother — Alzheimer’s disease diagnosed at 68, died in a nursing home. Occupation: head teacher. No cognitive testing or bloods on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked a video appointment herself for “a memory check”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia: assessment, management and support
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Lapses the patient notices herself, recalls in detail and that nobody else has seen, with intact complex function under heavy load, point to subjective cognitive concern rather than dementia. Still assess properly: reversible-cause bloods, a validated brief test as a dated baseline, and treat the load.

points.t: The question that does most of the work. Dementia usually shows as deficits that others notice and the patient minimises or forgets. Lapses spotted and logged by the patient, with no informant concern and intact complex work, fit subjective cognitive concern, most often driven by sleep, mood, alcohol or overload.

FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFTs, TFTs, B12 and folate. Screen for depression and anxiety, and take an alcohol history (AUDIT-C). Two glasses of wine most nights is well above the UK Chief Medical Officers’ 14 units a week (2016).

points.h: Use a validated brief test, and read it honestly
points.t: NICE NG97 names brief structured instruments for non-specialist settings, such as the 10-point cognitive screener (10-CS) and the 6-item cognitive impairment test (6CIT). It also warns that a normal score does not on its own rule dementia out. The baseline’s value lies in repeating it at a dated interval and comparing.

Refer to a specialist dementia diagnostic service when dementia is still suspected after reversible causes are excluded (NICE NG97). Change the lane if an informant notices decline, she has episodes she cannot recall, gets lost, repeats herself without knowing, her function slips, or there is focal neurology or rapid progression. At 62, any confirmed deficit is young-onset and needs specialist assessment.

One parent with Alzheimer’s diagnosed in her late sixties raises risk modestly and decides nothing. Autosomal dominant forms (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) are rare and usually present younger, and APOE testing has no clinical role outside research. If she wants a formal answer, a genetics referral is her choice.

Vasomotor symptoms and broken sleep since stopping HRT are treatable and affect concentration. NICE NG23 (updated April 2026): HRT does not appear to increase dementia risk, but it should not be offered to prevent dementia. Reopen HRT for her symptoms as an individual risk–benefit discussion.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her give all three episodes; acknowledged the request for a “real” test at once instead of deflecting.
Headship in an Ofsted year, 5-hour sleep, nightly wine, skipped meals, no holiday, and carrying it alone.
The notebook in shot, “eleven times”, and “they’d dress it as concern”: each explored, not passed over.
Idea (her mother’s Alzheimer’s starting again); concerns (six years of secret testing; losing her job); expectation (a real baseline and honest risk talk).
NICE NG97 reversible-cause bloods; validated brief cognitive test as dated baseline with a repeat; mood and alcohol screen.
Subjective cognitive concern from load vs early dementia; sleep deprivation, alcohol, menopause, anxiety, depression, thyroid, B12.
Asked about informant concern, unrecalled episodes, getting lost, repetition, functional decline and neurology.
Named the pattern as subjective concern under heavy load, explained why, and kept assessment open.
Bloods, baseline test with dated repeat, sleep and alcohol plan, HRT reopened, genetic counselling offered as her choice.
Vasomotor symptoms, alcohol above 14 units a week, sleep restriction and possible anxiety, each with an action.
Named the changes that would prompt earlier review; review in 6–8 weeks; repeat test dated.

social.t: A head teacher in an inspection year: sleep restriction, skipped meals, nightly alcohol to switch off and no holiday. These are modifiable drivers to negotiate, not lecture about.
Watching a mother go unheard with dementia, then six years of hidden self-testing; her husband doesn’t know. Isolation is part of the problem to address.

legal.t: Under the Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 an employer can get a GP report only with the patient’s written consent, and she can see it before it is sent. GMC Confidentiality (2017): disclosure to an employer without consent is not justified here.
If a long-term condition were ever diagnosed, it could count as a disability, with a duty on the employer to make reasonable adjustments. Worth knowing, not needed today.
No notification duty for subjective memory concern. A dementia diagnosis would need DVLA notification; that is not the situation now.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: take the concern seriously, investigate proportionately, and don’t give false reassurance. Share the reasoning for and against dementia openly.
Record accurately and neutrally (for example, “subjective memory concern; baseline cognitive assessment arranged”). Explain what is recorded and who can see it.

community.t: Education Support’s helpline for school staff, Alzheimer’s Society information on inherited risk, and NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) if anxiety persists.

redFlags: Others noticing decline; episodes she cannot recall; repeating herself without awareness
Getting lost somewhere familiar; function slipping at work or with finances
Focal neurology, personality change, or rapid progression over weeks — refer promptly
psychosocial: Inspection-year headship: 5-hour sleep, 4:45 waking, skipped lunch, no holiday
Nightly wine to switch off; flushes and night sweats since stopping HRT
Carrying it alone: husband unaware; fear for her job
ice: Idea: “It’s starting, the way it started with Mum.”
Concern: six years of secret self-testing; any record of “memory” will end her headship
Expectation: a real test, a baseline on paper, an honest risk conversation, and discretion

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Most likely subjective cognitive concern driven by sleep restriction, alcohol, vasomotor symptoms and heavy workload. Say so while still assessing properly: “Your pattern points away from dementia, and I want the tests to prove it.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “With dementia, the person usually doesn’t notice the slips and everyone else does. You noticed every one, remember them in detail, and nobody around you has seen a thing. That pattern is far more typical of an overloaded, underslept brain.”

management.reflectIce: “Nobody believed your mother until it was too late, so you made sure there would be evidence for you. I’m going to look properly, and put that evidence on paper.”
management.psychosocial: Answer the job fear precisely (confidentiality, consent for any employer report); agree one change she chooses (no wine on school nights); gently open the question of telling her husband.
sharedPlan: NICE NG97 bloods: FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFT, TFT, B12, folate
Validated brief cognitive test as a recorded baseline, with a repeat on a set date
Reopen HRT for vasomotor symptoms (NICE NG23); sleep and alcohol plan; genetic counselling if she wants it
safetyNet: Earlier review if others notice changes, unrecalled repetition, getting lost, or work slipping
Review in 6–8 weeks with results; repeat test dated

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: dismissing her or catastrophising. The marks go to the candidate who assesses properly, treats the load, and finds the notebook story and the job fear.

items.fail: “You’re running a school — you clearly don’t have dementia,” with no bloods and no test.
items.why: “Did not take the patient’s concern seriously.” Reassurance without assessment fails Tasks and confirms her worst belief about doctors.
items.fix: Assess properly: NICE NG97 bloods, a validated baseline, a dated repeat. Then reassurance carries weight.

items.fail: Straight to memory-clinic referral because of her mother, without exploring sleep, alcohol or menopause.
items.why: Reversible causes should be excluded first, and a referral on this history feeds the catastrophe.
items.fix: Name the load (five hours’ sleep, nightly wine, flushes since stopping HRT) and treat it; refer if anything objective emerges.

items.fail: Ignoring the notebook in shot and the “eleven times”.
items.why: “Did not pick up on cues.” Those are six years of secret fear showing on screen.
items.fix: “I can see your notebook — when did you start it?” Then acknowledge why she kept it.

items.fail: Never finding the governors fear, or answering it vaguely (“it’s all confidential”).
items.why: The employment terror is half the hidden agenda; a vague answer leaves it in place.
items.fix: Be precise: nothing is shared with work without her written consent, she can see any report first, and a normal baseline protects her.

items.fail: Quoting ACE-III, MoCA, APOE and PSEN1 at her without explaining.
items.why: “Used jargon.” She is clever, but frightened.
items.fix: Plain words: “a proper validated memory test”, “the strongly inherited forms are rare and start younger”.

items.fail: Ending with “come back if things get worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting leaves the notebook in charge of the watching.
items.fix: Name the specific changes, book the review, date the repeat test, and say you’ll take over the watching.
